raw:
The FDA defines the 'D&C Red lake blend' in a castor-oil carrier as follows:  
- The **lake** is classified as a straight color extended on a substratum by adsorption, coprecipitation, or chemical combination, and must meet specifications for soluble chlorides and sulfates (as sodium salts), not more than 3.0 percent, and ether extracts, not more than 0.5 percent; it is considered a straight color with the name derived from its base color and basic radical, as defined in §82.1051(b).  
- The **blend** is not explicitly defined or regulated under FDA definitions for lakes; however, since the term "blend" is not recognized in the definition of lake (which requires extension on a substratum by adsorption, coprecipitation, or chemical combination), and no such blend is described as being made by simple mixing, it may be considered outside the scope of the lake definition if composed solely of mixed components without substrate extension.  
- The **castor-oil carrier** is not defined in the provided sources as a substratum for a lake; therefore, the oil itself does not meet the criteria for a lake or any specified substrate under §82.1051. The term "lake" requires extension on a substratum such as alumina, blanc fixe, clay, or titanium dioxide, and castor oil is not listed among these substrata. Thus, if the oil serves only as a carrier without being part of the lake-forming process, it does not constitute a lake under FDA definition.

21 CFR 70.3(l) [10]: The term "lake" means a straight color extended on a substratum by adsorption, coprecipitation, or chemical combination that does not include any combination of ingredients made by simple mixing process.  
21 CFR 82.1051(a)(1) [1]: A lake is defined as one of the straight colors (except lakes) listed in subpart B or hereinbefore listed, which is a salt combined with sodium, potassium, aluminum, barium, calcium, strontium, or zirconium; this applies to the D&C Red lake blend if it results from extending a straight color on a substratum.  
21 CFR 82.1051(a)(2) [2]: Specifies that ether extracts shall not exceed 0.5 percent and soluble chlorides and sulfates (as sodium salts) shall not exceed 3.0 percent, which are requirements for the lake if it is certified under §82.1050.  
21 CFR 82.1051(a)(2) [3]: Specifies that intermediates shall not exceed 0.2 percent; this applies to any lake meeting the definition and specifications.  
21 CFR 82.1051(b) [4]: Each lake made as prescribed in paragraph (a) is considered a straight color and listed under a name formed according to specific rules.  
21 CFR 82.1051(b)(1) [5]: The listed name of the color from which the lake is prepared shall be used, with “FD&C” changed to “D&C” if present; for example, D&C Red No. 9—Barium Lake.  
21 CFR 82.1051(b)(2) [6]: The name includes the basic radical combined in such color (e.g., barium, aluminum).  
21 CFR 82.1051(b)(3) [7]: The word “Lake” is appended to the name; for example, D&C Red No. 9—Barium Lake.  
21 CFR 82.1051(b)(3) [8]: Provides an example of a lake name: D&C Green No. 1—Aluminum Lake, illustrating how the name is formed from base color and basic radical.  
21 CFR 82.1050 [9]: A batch of a straight color may be certified for use only in drugs and cosmetics if it conforms to §82.5 and the specifications set forth in this subpart; thus, certification applies only if the lake meets specified requirements including those in (a)(2).

raw:
Yes, Part 70 does address the use of colorants in new drug applications. For a tinted acne gel that includes an unlisted colorant purely for color, §70.10(b)(1) applies and requires that if such information has not previously been submitted and the safety of the color additive for the intended use has not already been established, the provisions of part 71 shall apply with respect to the information that must be submitted about the safety of the color additive [6]. This means that when a new drug application proposes the inclusion of a color additive for coloring purposes only, the applicant is required to submit safety data under part 71 regulations if such data has not been previously provided and the safety for the intended use has not already been established. The requirement depends on whether prior safety information was submitted or established.

21 CFR 70.10(b)(1) requires that, where a new drug application proposes the inclusion of a color additive for coloring purposes only, the provisions of part 71 shall apply with respect to the information that must be submitted about the safety of the color additive, if such information has not previously been submitted and the safety of the color additive for the intended use has not already been established [6].

21 CFR 70.10(b)(2) provides that if an application for a new drug inferentially contains a proposal for a color additive regulation and the applicant fails to designate it as such, the Commissioner shall notify the applicant and proceed in accordance with part 71 regulations [7]. This applies if the application does not explicitly state a request for a color additive regulation.

21 CFR 70.10(b)(3) states that where a petition for a color additive must be filed in accordance with paragraph (b)(2), the date of filing of the color additive petition shall be considered as the date of filing of the new-drug application [8]. This applies only if a separate petition is required under (b)(2).

These provisions do not establish that a colorant may be used without any safety evaluation; they require submission of safety information under part 71 when such data has not been previously provided and the use has not already been established. The regulations impose no requirement for pre-approval or specific labeling related to the colorant beyond the need to submit safety data as required by part 71, if applicable.

The available regulatory sources do not provide enough information to answer whether a tinted acne gel with an unlisted colorant used purely for color would be exempt from these requirements under any exception. The conditions in §70.10(b)(1) and (b)(2) are the only determinants, and they depend on prior submission of safety data or established safety.

asked: We're petitioning to list a new pigment for cosmetics. It shares a component with an already-listed colorant. Will FDA consider that overlap in setting a tolerance?
answer:
The FDA will consider overlap in setting a tolerance for a new pigment in cosmetics if the pigment shares a common component with an already-listed colorant, as long as that component is known to cause similar or related biological effects, and in the absence of evidence to the contrary, such components are presumed to have additive toxic effects. The Commissioner will take into consideration the amount of any common component permitted in other color additives, food additives, and pesticide chemical residues, as well as the similar biological activity produced by that substance when establishing tolerances.

21 CFR 70.11(a) states that different color additives may cause similar or related pharmacological or biological effects, and in the absence of evidence to the contrary, those that do so will be considered to have additive toxic effects [1].

21 CFR 70.11(b) states that food additives may also cause pharmacological or biological effects similar or related to such effects caused by color additives, and, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, those that do so will be considered as having additive toxic effects [2].

21 CFR 70.11(c) states that pesticide chemicals may also cause pharmacological or biological effects similar or related to such effects caused by color additives, and, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, those that do so will be considered to have additive toxic effects [3].

21 CFR 70.11(d) states that in establishing tolerances for color additives, the Commissioner will take into consideration, among other things, the amount of any common component permitted in other color additives, in food additives, and in pesticide chemical residues as well as the similar biological activity (such as cholinesterase inhibition) produced by such substance [4].

raw:
For a petition to list a new colorant for cosmetics only, the deposit due is $2,600.00, as specified in 21 CFR 70.19(c). If the petition is withdrawn before final acceptance for filing, the deposit shall be returned less a $600.00 fee for clerical handling and administrative and technical review, as stated in 21 CFR 70.19(e). This applies regardless of whether the withdrawal occurs within 30 days or after that period; however, if withdrawn within 30 days, a refund of $1,600.00 is due under 21 CFR 70.19(f), which would be less than the full deposit in this case since it applies only to petitions covered by paragraph (c). If the petition is withdrawn after filing and resubmitted within 6 months, a new deposit of $1,600.00 is required under 21 CFR 70.19(f), which would be less than the original deposit for cosmetics-only use. If the petition is resubmitted after 6 months, it shall be accompanied by the full deposit as if being submitted for the first time, per 21 CFR 70.19(g). For a withdrawal that occurs before acceptance for filing, a new advance deposit must be made in full as prescribed under paragraph (c), per 21 CFR 70.19(h).

21 CFR 70.19(a) [1]: Requires a $3,000.00 deposit if the proposal is for listing the color additive for use generally in or on foods, in or on drugs, and in or on cosmetics.  
21 CFR 70.19(b) [2]: Requires a $3,000.00 deposit if the petition is for use in or on foods only.  
21 CFR 70.19(c) [3]: Requires a $2,600.00 deposit if the petition is for use in or on drugs and/or cosmetics only.  
21 CFR 70.19(d) [4]: States that the provisions of paragraphs (a), (b), and (c) apply regardless of whether tolerances, limitations, or restrictions are contemplated.  
21 CFR 70.19(e) [5]: If a petition is withdrawn before final acceptance for filing, the deposit shall be returned less a $600.00 fee for clerical handling and administrative and technical review.  
21 CFR 70.19(f) [6]: If a petition is withdrawn within 30 days after filing, the deposit shall be returned less $1,800.00 if under (a) or (b), or $1,600.00 if under (c).  
21 CFR 70.19(g) [7]: If a petition is withdrawn and resubmitted within 6 months, it shall be accompanied by a deposit of $1,800.00 for (a) or (b), or $1,600.00 for (c); if resubmitted after 6 months, the full deposit required at first filing applies.  
21 CFR 70.19(h) [8]: If a petition is withdrawn before acceptance and then resubmitted, a new advance deposit shall be made in full as prescribed under (a), (b), or (c).  
21 CFR 70.19(i) [9]: After listing, an amendment or additional tolerance request requires $1,800.00 for use in foods/drugs or $1,600.00 for cosmetics only.  
21 CFR 70.19(j) [10]: A fee of $250.00 is required for listing a diluent under §80.35 for color additive mixtures.  
21 CFR 70.19(k) [11]: Objections or requests for public hearing require a filing fee of $250.00.  
21 CFR 70.19(l) [12]: If a petition is referred to an advisory committee, the petitioner bears all related costs including personal compensation at not more than $75 per member per day.  
21 CFR 70.19(m) [13]: A special advance deposit of $2,500.00 is required for referrals to advisory committees; further deposits may be made upon request and any excess over actual expenses will be refunded.  
21 CFR 70.19(n) [14]: Requests for pharmacological or scientific studies require an advance deposit of $5,000.00, with possible additional deposits if needed and refunds of excess amounts.  
21 CFR 70.19(o) [15]: A petition for judicial review shall pay the costs to prepare a transcript of the record.  
21 CFR 70.19(p) [16]: All deposits and fees must be paid by money order, bank draft, or certified check drawn to the FDA, and forwarded to HFS-200 in College Park, MD.

asked: We repack certified straight colors into smaller pails for cosmetic customers. What packaging rules apply?
answer:
Repackaging certified straight colors into smaller pails for cosmetic customers is permitted under the following conditions: the packaging must prevent changes in composition, be sealed so they cannot be opened without breaking the seal, and any unavoidable change in moisture content due to ordinary exposure during storage, packing, or distribution does not constitute a change in composition. If the packaging material is a food additive, it must be authorized by an appropriate regulation in parts 170 through 189 of this chapter. The term "straight color" includes lakes and substances permitted by specifications for such colors as defined in parts 73, 74, and 81 of this chapter.

21 CFR 70.3(j) [2] defines the term "straight color" to include color additives listed in parts 73, 74, and 81 of this chapter, and such substances as lakes and those permitted by specifications for these colors.

21 CFR 70.20 [1] requires that straight colors be packaged in containers which prevent changes in composition; the packages must be sealed so they cannot be opened without breaking the seal; an unavoidable change in moisture content due to ordinary and customary exposure during good storage, packing, and distribution practice is not considered a change in composition; if the packaging material is a food additive, it shall be authorized by an appropriate regulation in parts 170 through 189 of this chapter.

When a cosmetic use is included in a petition alongside food uses and the data do not demonstrate that all proposed levels are safe, the safety of the product has not been determined, and a warning must be included on the principal display panel: "Warning—The safety of this product has not been determined" [2]. This applies unless three conditions are met: (1) the safety had been adequately substantiated prior to development of new information; (2) the new information does not demonstrate a hazard to human health; and (3) adequate studies are being conducted to determine expeditiously the safety of the ingredient or product [5], [6]. If these conditions are met, the warning required under paragraph (a) is not needed for that ingredient or product [3].

The requirement in 21 CFR 740.10(a) mandates a conspicuous statement on the principal display panel if the safety of the product has not been adequately substantiated prior to marketing: "Warning—The safety of this product has not been determined" [2].  

The requirement in 21 CFR 740.10(b)(1) states that the warning is not required if the safety had been adequately substantiated prior to development of new information [4].  

The requirement in 21 CFR 740.10(b)(2) specifies that the warning is not required if the new information does not demonstrate a hazard to human health [5].

asked: If FDA grants our petition for a new cosmetic color, what will the listing regulation look like and when will it publish?
answer:
If FDA grants a petition for a new cosmetic color, the listing regulation will be published in the Federal Register within 90 days after filing of the petition (or within 180 days if extended as provided in section 721(d)(1) of the act). The regulation will list the color additive in part 73 or 74 of this chapter on the appropriate list or lists, and it may specify the conditions under which the color additive may be safely used, including maximum quantities, specific food, drug, or cosmetic uses, methods of addition, and labeling requirements deemed necessary to assure safety. The regulation will only list the color additive for the use(s) for which it has been found suitable and safe; if not, the Commissioner shall by order deny the petition and notify the petitioner of such order and reasons. If the color additive is intended for use in meat, meat food product, or poultry product subject to FMIA or PPIA, the regulation must list any such uses where the color has been found suitable and safe. The regulation may exempt the color additive from batch certification if the Commissioner finds it unnecessary for public health protection, based on considerations of composition, manufacturing process, impurities, toxic potential, control procedures, and variability.

21 CFR 70.3(j) [7] defines "straight color" as a color additive listed in parts 73, 74, and 81 of this chapter, including lakes and substances permitted by the specifications for such color.

21 CFR 71.20(a) [2] requires that the regulation list the color additive in part 73 or 74 of this chapter on an appropriate list or lists as provided under section 721(b)(1).

21 CFR 71.20(a)(1) [3] specifies that the regulation may list the color additive for general use in or on foods, drugs, or cosmetics, or for coloring the human body, and may prescribe conditions such as maximum quantities of straight color or diluent, specific food, drug, or cosmetic classes, methods of addition, and labeling or packing requirements to assure safety.

21 CFR 71.20(a)(2) [4] requires that the regulation list the color additive only for uses for which it has been found suitable and safe; alternatively, the Commissioner may deny the petition with reasons.

21 CFR 71.20(a)(3) [5] mandates that if the color is to be used in meat, meat food product, or poultry product under FMIA or PPIA, the regulation must list such uses where the color has been found suitable and safe.

21 CFR 71.20(b) [6] provides that the Commissioner may exempt the color additive from batch certification if they find it unnecessary for public health protection, based on composition, manufacturing process, possible impurities, toxic potential, control and analytical procedures, and variability of composition.

asked: We want to ship test mascaras containing an unlisted color additive to an outside safety lab. Is there an exemption, and what labeling and records are required?
answer:
Yes, shipping test mascaras containing an unlisted color additive to an outside safety lab is permitted under an exemption, provided that the shipment meets specific labeling and recordkeeping requirements. The exemption applies only if the product bears a label stating prominently: “Caution—Contains new color additive—For investigational use only,” and the shipment is delivered by experts qualified to determine safety [1]. This exemption does not apply unless the conditions in §71.37(a) are met, including that no animals used in such investigations or their products (e.g., milk, eggs) shall be used for food purposes without prior authorization from the FDA based on public health data [1].

The labeling required is a prominently displayed statement: “Caution—Contains new color additive—For investigational use only” on the container of the mascara containing the unlisted color additive [1].

The person responsible for shipping or delivering the product must maintain adequate records that include the name and post-office address of the expert to whom the color additive is shipped, the date, quantity, and batch or code mark of each shipment or delivery, and these records must be kept for a period of 2 years after such shipment and delivery [2]. These records must be available for inspection and copying upon request by a properly authorized employee of the FDA at reasonable times [2].

asked: We're launching a blush colored with carmine. May we use it, and does carmine need to be declared on the label?
answer:
Yes, carmine may be used in a blush product intended for use on the face, including areas near the eyes, as long as it is used in accordance with good manufacturing practices and does not violate any restrictions on use in the area of the eye. However, because the blush contains carmine and is intended for use in or near the area of the eye, labeling requirements apply. The use of carmine in a blush is permitted under 21 CFR 73.2087(b), which allows carmine to be safely used in cosmetics generally, including those intended for use in the area of the eye, provided good manufacturing practices are followed [2]. Additionally, because the product contains carmine and is not subject to the requirements of § 701.3, it must specifically declare the presence of carmine prominently and conspicuously at least once in the labeling, as required by 21 CFR 73.2087(c)(2) [5]. This requirement applies regardless of whether the product is intended for use on or near the eyes, since the term "area of the eye" includes the eyelids and surrounding skin [7].

21 CFR 70.3(s) defines the area of the eye as the region enclosed within the supra-orbital and infra-orbital ridges, including the eyebrow, skin below the eyebrow, eyelids, eyelashes, conjunctival sac, eyeball, and soft areolar tissue [7].

21 CFR 73.2087(a) requires that carmine conform in identity and specifications to the requirements of § 73.100(a)(2) and (b)(2) [1].

21 CFR 73.2087(b) permits the use of carmine in cosmetics generally, including those intended for use in the area of the eye, provided it is used in amounts consistent with good manufacturing practices [2].

21 CFR 73.2087(c) establishes labeling requirements for carmine-containing products [3].

21 CFR 73.2087(c)(1) requires that any color additive or mixture prepared therefrom intended solely or in part for coloring purposes shall bear labeling in accordance with the provisions of § 70.25 [4].

21 CFR 73.2087(c)(2) mandates that cosmetics containing carmine not subject to the requirements of § 701.3 must specifically declare the presence of carmine prominently and conspicuously at least once in the labeling, such as “Contains carmine as a color additive” [5].

21 CFR 73.2087(d) exempts batches of carmine from certification because certification is not necessary for public health protection [6].

asked: We make a progressive hair-color cream for men's gray hair using bismuth citrate. What are the use limits, warnings, and certification status?

There is no mention of FD&C Blue No. 1 or its aluminum lake in any provision listed. Therefore, based on the evidence provided, neither FD&C Blue No. 1 nor FD&C Blue No. 1 Aluminum Lake is authorized for use in eye shadow under the cited provisions.

21 CFR 70.3(s) [9] defines the "area of the eye" as including the skin below the eyebrow, eyelids, eyelashes, conjunctival sac, eyeball, and soft tissue within the infra-orbital ridge — this definition applies to any color additive used in that area, but does not specify which dyes are permitted.

21 CFR 74.2340(a) [1] specifies identity and specifications for FD&C Red No. 40; it does not address Blue dyes or their lakes.

21 CFR 74.2340(a)(1) [2] requires that FD&C Red No. 40 conform to the requirements of § 74.340(a)(1) and (b); this applies only to red dye, not blue.

21 CFR 74.2340(a)(2) [3] allows lakes prepared as described in §§ 82.51 and 82.1051, except that the color additive used is FD&C Red No. 40 — this restriction applies only to red dyes and does not extend to blue.

21 CFR 74.2340(b) [4] restricts use of FD&C Red No. 40 in eye area products to only FD&C Red No. 40 and its aluminum lake, with exceptions noted in (b)(1) and (b)(2); this restriction does not apply to blue dyes.

21 CFR 74.2340(b)(1) [5] requires that amounts used be consistent with current good manufacturing practice — a general requirement for all color additives in cosmetics, but not specific to blue dyes or eye use.

21 CFR 74.2340(b)(2) [6] prohibits exposure of the color additive to oxidizing or reducing agents that may affect integrity — this applies generally and does not specify which dyes are affected.

21 CFR 74.2340(c) [7] requires labeling in accordance with § 70.25 — a general requirement for all color additives, regardless of type.

21 CFR 74.2340(d) [8] mandates certification of batches according to part 80 regulations — applies generally and not specifically to blue dyes.

The available regulatory sources do not provide any authorization or restriction on the use of FD&C Blue No. 1 or FD&C Blue No. 1 Aluminum Lake in eye shadow, nor do they specify conditions under which such dyes may be used in the area of the eye. Therefore, based solely on the provided text, neither dye is permitted for use in eye shadow formulations.

asked: We're a small skincare brand formulating a tinted body lotion. Our supplier offers D&C Blue No. 4. Can we use it, is there a use limit, and does the color need FDA certification?
answer:
Body lotion: permitted.
21 CFR 74.2104(b) states: "D&C Blue No. 4 may be safely used for coloring externally applied cosmetics in amounts consistent with good manufacturing practice." [2].
Use limit: no percentage is stated; the amount is consistent with good manufacturing practice [2].
21 CFR 74.2104(a) states: "The color additive D&C Blue No. 4 shall conform in identity and specifications to the requirements of § 74.1104(a)(1) and (b)." [1].
21 CFR 74.2104(c) states: "The label of the color additive shall conform to the requirements of § 70.25 of this chapter." [3].
21 CFR 74.2104(d) states: "All batches of D&C Blue No. 4 shall be certified in accordance with regulations in part 80 of this chapter." [4].
21 CFR 82.1104 states: "The color additive D&C Blue No. 4 shall conform in identity and specifications to the requirements of § 74.1104(a)(1) and (b) of this chapter. D&C Blue No. 4 is restricted to use in externally applied drugs and cosmetics." [5].
21 CFR 70.3(v) states: "The terms externally applied drugs and externally applied cosmetics mean drugs or cosmetics applied only to external parts of the body and not to the lips or any body surface covered by mucous membrane." [6].
21 CFR 82.1050 states: "A batch of a straight color listed in this subpart may be certified, in accordance with the provisions of this part, for use only in drugs and cosmetics, if such batch conforms to the requirements of § 82.5 and to the specifications set forth in this subpart for such color." [7].

The sample sent with a certification request must be taken only after the batch has been thoroughly mixed to ensure uniform composition throughout [2], and must be held under the control of the person requesting certification until certified [3]. The sample must be labeled to show: (1) the name of the color additive [5], (2) the manufacturer's batch number [6], (3) the quantity of such batch [7], (4) the name and post-office address of the person requesting certification of such batch [8], and (5) be accompanied by any label or labeling intended to be used [9].

The name of the color additive is required and must be shown on the sample label [5].  
The manufacturer's batch number is required and must be shown on the sample label [6].  
The quantity of such batch is required and must be shown on the sample label [7].  
The name and post-office address of the person requesting certification are required and must be shown on the sample label [8].  
Any label or labeling intended to be used must accompany the sample [9].  

The requirement that the batch be thoroughly mixed prior to sampling applies only if the batch has been properly mixed [2]. The sample must remain under the control of the requester until certification is issued [3].

asked: FDA suspended certification service to our company after a records audit. On what grounds can it do that, and what can we do?
answer:
The FDA can suspend certification service to a company if it appears to the Commissioner that the person has: (1) obtained or attempted to obtain a certificate through fraud or misrepresentation of a material fact; (2) falsified records required to be kept under § 80.39; (3) failed to keep such records, make them available, or allow inventory checks as required by § 80.39; or (4) refused to permit duly authorized FDA employees free access to manufacturing facilities, processes, and formulae involved in the manufacture of color additives and intermediates from which such color additives are derived [1]. The grounds for suspension are specifically listed in 21 CFR 80.34(a)(1) through (a)(4), with each condition being a basis upon which the Commissioner may suspend certification service. A person who contests the suspension has an opportunity for a regulatory hearing before the FDA pursuant to part 16 of this chapter [6].

21 CFR 80.34(a)(1): The FDA can suspend certification service if it appears that a person obtained or attempted to obtain a certificate through fraud or misrepresentation of a material fact [2].  
21 CFR 80.34(a)(2): The FDA can suspend certification service if the person falsified the records required to be kept under § 80.39 [3].  
21 CFR 80.34(a)(3): The FDA can suspend certification service if the person failed to keep such records, make them available, or allow full opportunity for inventory checks as required by § 80.39 [4].  
21 CFR 80.34(a)(4): The FDA can suspend certification service if the person refused to permit duly authorized FDA employees free access to all manufacturing facilities, processes, and formulae involved in the manufacture of color additives and intermediates from which such color additives are derived [5].  
21 CFR 80.34(b): Any person who contests a suspension of service has an opportunity for a regulatory hearing before the FDA pursuant to part 16 of this chapter [6].

asked: We hold certificates for our color batches. What distribution records must we keep, and for how long?
answer:
We must keep distribution records for color additive batches covered by certificates. The records must show: (1) each quantity used from the batch, including the date and kind of use; and (2) the date and quantity of each shipment or delivery, along with the name and post-office address of the recipient. These records must be kept separately from all other records. They must be made available to FDA or any officer acting on behalf of the Secretary of Health and Human Services at all reasonable hours until at least 2 years after the disposal of all such color additive [1].  

21 CFR 80.39(b)(1) requires that each quantity used from a batch be recorded, along with the date and kind of such use [3].  
21 CFR 80.39(b)(2) requires that the date and quantity of each shipment or delivery be recorded, including the name and post-office address of the person to whom it was delivered [4].  
21 CFR 80.39(a) requires that records be made available until at least 2 years after disposal of all such color additive [1].  
21 CFR 80.39(c) requires that the records required by paragraph (a) be kept separately from all other records [5].

asked: An old formula of ours uses FD&C Red No. 4 in a lipstick and a body lotion. Is FD&C Red No. 4 still usable?
answer:
Lipstick: not permitted.
21 CFR 74.2304(b) states: "FD&C Red No. 4 may be safely used for coloring externally applied cosmetics in amounts consistent with good manufacturing practice." [2].
21 CFR 70.3(v) states: "The terms externally applied drugs and externally applied cosmetics mean drugs or cosmetics applied only to external parts of the body and not to the lips or any body surface covered by mucous membrane." [6].
Body lotion: permitted.
Use limit: no percentage is stated; the amount is consistent with good manufacturing practice [2].
21 CFR 74.2304(a) states: "The color additive FD&C Red No. 4 shall conform in identity and specifications to the requirements of § 74.1304(a)(1) and (b)." [1].
21 CFR 74.2304(c) states: "The label of the color additive shall conform to the requirements of § 70.25 of this chapter." [3].
21 CFR 74.2304(d) states: "All batches of FD&C Red No. 4 shall be certified in accordance with regulations in part 80 of this chapter." [4].
21 CFR 82.304 states: "The color additive FD&C Red No. 4 shall conform in identity and specifications to the requirements of § 74.1304(a)(1) and (b) of this chapter. FD&C Red No. 4 is restricted to use in externally applied drugs and cosmetics." [5].
21 CFR 82.50 states: "A batch of a straight color listed in this subpart may be certified, in accordance with the provisions of the regulations in this part, for use in food, drugs, and cosmetics, if such batch conforms to the requirements of § 82.5 and to the specifications in this subpart set forth for such color." [7].

asked: What general specifications must a batch of an FD&C (subpart B) straight color meet before it can be certified?
answer:
A batch of an FD&C (subpart B) straight color must meet the following general specifications before it can be certified:  
- It must be free from all impurities, except those specifically named in paragraph (b) or in the specifications for that color, to the extent such impurities can be avoided by good manufacturing practice [2].  
- For a straight color listed in subpart B, lead (as Pb) shall not exceed 0.001 percent [5]; arsenic (as As₂O₃) shall not exceed 0.00014 percent [6]; and heavy metals (except Pb and As), by precipitation as sulfides, shall not exceed trace levels [7].  
- For a straight color listed in subpart C or D, lead (as Pb) shall not exceed 0.002 percent [9]; arsenic (as As₂O₃) shall not exceed 0.0002 percent [10]; and heavy metals (except Pb and As), by precipitation as sulfides, shall not exceed 0.003 percent [11].  
- If the straight color contains a barium salt listed in subpart C or D, soluble barium (in dilute HCl) as BaCl₂ shall not exceed 0.05 percent [12].  

The batch must also conform to the general specifications outlined in section (b), which differ based on whether the color is listed in subpart B, C, or D [3], and specifically for subpart B, the limits on lead, arsenic, and heavy metals are as defined above.  

21 CFR 70.3(j) [13] defines "straight color" as a color additive listed in parts 73, 74, and 81 of this chapter, including lakes and substances permitted by the specifications for such color.  

21 CFR 82.5(a) [2] requires that the batch be free from all impurities (other than those named in paragraph (b) or in the specifications set forth therein) to the extent such impurities can be avoided by good manufacturing practice.  

21 CFR 82.5(b) [3] specifies that the batch must conform to the following:  
- For subpart B, lead not more than 0.001 percent [5]; arsenic not more than 0.00014 percent [6]; and heavy metals (except Pb and As) not more than trace [7].  
- For subpart C or D, lead not more than 0.002 percent [9]; arsenic not more than 0.0002 percent [10]; and heavy metals (except Pb and As) not more than 0.003 percent [11].  
- For a straight color containing a barium salt in subpart C or D, soluble barium (as BaCl₂) not more than 0.05 percent [12].  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(1) [4] applies specifically to straight colors listed in subpart B and sets the limits on lead, arsenic, and heavy metals as specified in subsections (b)(1)(i), (b)(1)(ii), and (b)(1)(iii).  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(1)(i) [5] requires that lead (as Pb) not exceed 0.001 percent for a straight color listed in subpart B.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(1)(ii) [6] requires that arsenic (as As₂O₃) not exceed 0.00014 percent for a straight color listed in subpart B.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(1)(iii) [7] requires that heavy metals (except Pb and As), by precipitation as sulfides, not exceed trace levels for a straight color listed in subpart B, except that this limit is subject to the condition that such impurities are not present beyond what can be avoided by good manufacturing practice.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(2) [8] applies to straight colors listed in subpart C or D and specifies different limits for lead, arsenic, and heavy metals than those for subpart B.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(2)(i) [9] requires that lead (as Pb) not exceed 0.002 percent for a straight color listed in subpart C or D.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(2)(ii) [10] requires that arsenic (as As₂O₃) not exceed 0.0002 percent for a straight color listed in subpart C or D.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(2)(iii) [11] requires that heavy metals (except Pb and As), by precipitation as sulfides, not exceed 0.003 percent for a straight color listed in subpart C or D.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(3) [12] specifies that if the straight color contains a barium salt listed in subpart C or D, soluble barium (in dilute HCl) as BaCl₂ shall not exceed 0.05 percent.  

21 CFR 70.3(j) [13] defines "straight color" to include lakes and substances permitted by the specifications for such color, which is relevant to determining whether a substance qualifies as a straight color under FD&C subpart B.

raw:
A batch of an FD&C (subpart B) straight color must meet the following general specifications before it can be certified:  
- It must be free from all impurities, except those specifically named in paragraph (b) or in the specifications for that color, to the extent such impurities can be avoided by good manufacturing practice [2].  
- For a straight color listed in subpart B, lead (as Pb) shall not exceed 0.001 percent [5]; arsenic (as As₂O₃) shall not exceed 0.00014 percent [6]; and heavy metals (except Pb and As), by precipitation as sulfides, shall not exceed trace levels [7].  
- For a straight color listed in subpart C or D, lead (as Pb) shall not exceed 0.002 percent [9]; arsenic (as As₂O₃) shall not exceed 0.0002 percent [10]; and heavy metals (except Pb and As), by precipitation as sulfides, shall not exceed 0.003 percent [11].  
- If the straight color contains a barium salt listed in subpart C or D, soluble barium (in dilute HCl) as BaCl₂ shall not exceed 0.05 percent [12].  

The batch must also conform to the general specifications outlined in section (b), which differ based on whether the color is listed in subpart B, C, or D [3], and specifically for subpart B, the limits on lead, arsenic, and heavy metals are as defined above.  

21 CFR 70.3(j) [13] defines "straight color" as a color additive listed in parts 73, 74, and 81 of this chapter, including lakes and substances permitted by the specifications for such color.  

21 CFR 82.5(a) [2] requires that the batch be free from all impurities (other than those named in paragraph (b) or in the specifications set forth therein) to the extent such impurities can be avoided by good manufacturing practice.  

21 CFR 82.5(b) [3] specifies that the batch must conform to the following:  
- For subpart B, lead not more than 0.001 percent [5]; arsenic not more than 0.00014 percent [6]; and heavy metals (except Pb and As) not more than trace [7].  
- For subpart C or D, lead not more than 0.002 percent [9]; arsenic not more than 0.0002 percent [10]; and heavy metals (except Pb and As) not more than 0.003 percent [11].  
- For a straight color containing a barium salt in subpart C or D, soluble barium (as BaCl₂) not more than 0.05 percent [12].  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(1) [4] applies specifically to straight colors listed in subpart B and sets the limits on lead, arsenic, and heavy metals as specified in subsections (b)(1)(i), (b)(1)(ii), and (b)(1)(iii).  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(1)(i) [5] requires that lead (as Pb) not exceed 0.001 percent for a straight color listed in subpart B.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(1)(ii) [6] requires that arsenic (as As₂O₃) not exceed 0.00014 percent for a straight color listed in subpart B.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(1)(iii) [7] requires that heavy metals (except Pb and As), by precipitation as sulfides, not exceed trace levels for a straight color listed in subpart B, except that this limit is subject to the condition that such impurities are not present beyond what can be avoided by good manufacturing practice.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(2) [8] applies to straight colors listed in subpart C or D and specifies different limits for lead, arsenic, and heavy metals than those for subpart B.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(2)(i) [9] requires that lead (as Pb) not exceed 0.002 percent for a straight color listed in subpart C or D.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(2)(ii) [10] requires that arsenic (as As₂O₃) not exceed 0.0002 percent for a straight color listed in subpart C or D.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(2)(iii) [11] requires that heavy metals (except Pb and As), by precipitation as sulfides, not exceed 0.003 percent for a straight color listed in subpart C or D.  

21 CFR 82.5(b)(3) [12] specifies that if the straight color contains a barium salt listed in subpart C or D, soluble barium (in dilute HCl) as BaCl₂ shall not exceed 0.05 percent.  

21 CFR 70.3(j) [13] defines "straight color" to include lakes and substances permitted by the specifications for such color, which is relevant to determining whether a substance qualifies as a straight color under FD&C subpart B.

asked: We want to make FD&C aluminum lakes for cosmetics. What does the regulation require for composition, specifications and naming?
answer:
The regulation requires that FD&C aluminum lakes for cosmetics be prepared by extending a certified water-soluble straight color on an alumina substratum, and each such lake must meet specific composition and specification criteria, including limits on soluble chlorides and sulfates and inorganic matter. The name of the lake is determined by combining the listed name of the parent color with the name of the basic radical (aluminum) and appending the word “Lake.” These lakes are considered straight colors and must conform to specifications set forth for the parent color, including those in §82.50.

21 CFR 82.51(a)(1) [1] requires that any aluminum lake be made by extending a salt derived from one of the certified water-soluble straight colors on an alumina substratum using either the aluminum or calcium basic radical.

21 CFR 82.51(a)(2) [2] specifies that lakes must be prepared from previously certified colors listed in this subpart, and further limits soluble chlorides and sulfates (as sodium salts) to not more than 2.0 percent; insoluble HCl and inorganic matter are limited to not more than 0.5 percent [3].

21 CFR 82.51(b) [4] establishes that each lake made as prescribed in paragraph (a) shall be considered a straight color and listed under a name formed according to specific rules.

21 CFR 82.51(b)(1) [5] requires the name of the lake to include the listed name of the parent color from which it is prepared.

21 CFR 82.51(b)(2) [6] requires the inclusion of the name of the basic radical (aluminum or calcium) combined in the color.

21 CFR 82.51(b)(3) [7] and [8] require that the word “Lake” be appended to the name, as illustrated by the example: FD&C Blue No. 1—Aluminum Lake.

21 CFR 82.50 [9] requires a batch of a straight color (including lakes) to be certified for use in food, drugs, and cosmetics if it conforms to §82.5 and to the specifications set forth in this subpart for that color.

asked: We're launching a lipstick and a fluoride-free toothpaste, both colored with D&C Orange No. 5. What limits apply under Part 82?
answer:
21 CFR 70.3(v) [3] defines "externally applied drugs and externally applied cosmetics" as substances applied only to external parts of the body and not to the lips or any body surface covered by mucous membrane, thereby excluding lipsticks and toothpastes because both are applied to mucous membrane surfaces.

21 CFR 82.1255(a) [1] requires that D&C Orange No. 5 conform in identity and specifications to §74.1255(a)(1) and (b).

21 CFR 82.1255(b) [2] limits the use of D&C Orange No. 5 to no more than 5.0 percent by weight in lipsticks and other cosmetics applied to the lips, and to amounts consistent with current good manufacturing practice in mouthwashes, dentifrices, and externally applied cosmetics.

21 CFR 82.1050 [4] requires that a batch of D&C Orange No. 5 used in drugs or cosmetics must conform to the requirements of §82.5 and to the specifications set forth in this subpart for such color.

raw:
The use of D&C Orange No. 5 in a lipstick and a fluoride-free toothpaste is permitted under specific conditions outlined in the provided regulations.

For the lipstick:  
D&C Orange No. 5 may be used in amounts not exceeding 5.0 percent by weight of the finished cosmetic product, as long as it is applied to the lips, which are considered external body surfaces covered by mucous membranes. However, since lipsticks are applied to the lips—specifically a mucous membrane-covered surface—the use of D&C Orange No. 5 in such products is restricted under §82.1255(b), which limits its use for coloring lipsticks to no more than 5.0 percent by weight. This restriction applies only if the product is considered an externally applied cosmetic, as defined in §70.3(v). The definition of "externally applied cosmetics" excludes application to the lips or mucous membranes, so this creates a conflict: since lipsticks are applied to the lips (a mucous membrane surface), they fall outside the scope of "externally applied cosmetics" as defined in 21 CFR 70.3(v). Therefore, D&C Orange No. 5 cannot be used in lipsticks under §82.1255(b) because lipsticks are not considered externally applied cosmetics per §70.3(v), and the restriction on use for lipsticks is conditional upon being an externally applied cosmetic.

For the fluoride-free toothpaste:  
D&C Orange No. 5 may be used in amounts consistent with current good manufacturing practice, as long as it is used in dentifrices (toothpastes) intended for external application. Since toothpaste is applied to the mouth and not directly on mucous membranes, and since it is a dentifrice, it falls under the category of externally applied cosmetics. However, §70.3(v) defines "externally applied cosmetics" as those applied only to external parts of the body and not to the lips or any body surface covered by mucous membrane. Toothpaste is applied in the mouth, which includes mucous membranes, so it does not meet the definition of an externally applied cosmetic under §70.3(v). Therefore, D&C Orange No. 5 cannot be used in toothpastes as a result.

Thus, based on the definitions and restrictions:
- The lipstick use of D&C Orange No. 5 is not permitted because lipsticks are applied to mucous membranes (lips), which fall outside the definition of "externally applied cosmetics" under §70.3(v).
- The toothpaste use of D&C Orange No. 5 is not permitted because toothpastes are applied to mucous membrane surfaces in the mouth, and thus do not qualify as externally applied cosmetics under §70.3(v).

asked: We plan a calcium lake of an Ext. D&C color on clay for a body glitter. What does Part 82 require for an Ext. D&C lake?
answer:
Part 82 requires that an Ext. D&C lake made on a clay substratum using calcium as the basic radical is permitted, provided it meets the specifications for lakes defined under §82.2051. The lake must be prepared by extending one of the straight colors (e.g., Ext. D&C Yellow No. 2) with calcium and applied to a substratum such as clay; however, the specific color or type of lake is not restricted by the substrate alone—only that the preparation follows the general rules for lakes in §82.2051.

21 CFR 82.2051(a)(1) [1] permits lakes made from a straight color (e.g., Ext. D&C Yellow No. 2) extended on substrata such as clay, titanium dioxide, or zinc oxide, provided the lake is formed by combining the basic radical calcium with one of the listed straight colors.

21 CFR 82.2051(a)(2) [2] and [3] require that ether extracts shall not exceed 0.5 percent; soluble chlorides and sulfates (as sodium salts) shall not exceed 3.0 percent; and intermediates shall not exceed 0.2 percent.

21 CFR 82.2051(b) [4] states each lake made as prescribed in paragraph (a) is considered a straight color and listed under the name formed by combining the original color name, the basic radical used, and the word “Lake.”

21 CFR 82.2051(b)(1) [5] requires that the listed name of the color from which the lake is prepared be included in the name.

21 CFR 82.2051(b)(2) [6] requires that the name of the basic radical combined in such color (e.g., calcium) be included in the name.

21 CFR 82.2051(b)(3) [7] requires that the word “Lake” be appended to the name, as in "Ext. D&C Yellow No. 2—Calcium Lake."

21 CFR 82.2050 [8] requires a batch of a straight color (including lakes) to conform to §82.5 and to the specifications set forth in this subpart for such color to be certified for use in externally applied drugs and cosmetics.

asked: We're reformulating an antibacterial body wash and a supplier offers bithionol. Can we use it at a low level?
answer:
No, bithionol cannot be used in the antibacterial body wash, regardless of the level, because bithionol is deemed to render any cosmetic product containing it injurious to users under 21 CFR 700.11(a). The regulation states that bithionol is a deleterious substance and any cosmetic containing it is considered adulterated [1].

21 CFR 700.11(a) prohibits the use of bithionol in cosmetics due to its potential to cause photosensitivity in humans, with possible persistent severe reactions, and risk of cross-sensitization with other chemicals like certain halogenated salicylanilides and hexachlorophene [1].  

21 CFR 700.11(b) provides that regulatory proceedings may be initiated for any cosmetic preparation containing bithionol shipped after March 15, 1968 [2].

asked: We sell a mouthwash on open drugstore shelves. Do we need tamper-resistant packaging?
answer:
Yes, you need tamper-resistant packaging for your mouthwash sold on open drugstore shelves because the product is a cosmetic liquid oral hygiene product accessible to the public while held for sale [2].  

The requirement applies if the mouthwash is packaged for retail sale and is accessible to the public during retail display; the package must have an indicator or barrier to entry that provides visible evidence of tampering if breached or missing, and this feature must be distinctive by design—meaning it cannot be duplicated with commonly available materials or processes—and must remain intact when handled in a reasonable manner during manufacture, distribution, and retail display [2].  

A prominent labeling statement is required on each retail package (except aerosol products) that alerts consumers to the specific tamper-resistant feature of the package, and this statement must remain visible even if the tamper-resistant feature is breached or missing. If the tamper-resistant feature uses an identifying characteristic (e.g., a pattern, name, logo), that characteristic must be referenced in the labeling statement [3].  

The tamper-resistant packaging requirement is effective on February 7, 1983 for products packaged for retail sale on or after that date, except for vaginal tablets, and is effective on May 5, 1983 for vaginal tablets; the full requirements, including a distinctive indicator by design and labeling statement, are effective on May 5, 1983 for all affected cosmetic products, with the specific reference to identifying characteristics becoming effective on February 6, 1984 [10][12]. The requirement is also effective on or after February 6, 1984 for products held for sale on or after that date [13].  

The requirement does not apply to aerosol products, which are defined as those depending on liquefied or compressed gas to expel contents [2].  

An exemption from the packaging and labeling requirements may be requested through a citizen petition under §700.25(d), which must include the name of the product, reasons that compliance is unnecessary or unachievable, and other information justifying an exemption [5][6][7].  

The requirement applies to all cosmetic liquid oral hygiene products accessible to the public while held for sale; it does not apply to products not accessible to the public during retail display [2].

Yes, you need tamper-resistant packaging for your mouthwash sold on open drugstore shelves because the product is a cosmetic liquid oral hygiene product accessible to the public while held for sale [21 CFR 700.25(b)]. This requirement applies unless an exemption has been granted under §700.25(d) [2].

The requirement for tamper-resistant packaging applies to mouthwash if it is sold for retail sale and is accessible to the public during retail display, as defined in section (b) of 21 CFR 700.25 [2]. The package must have an indicator or barrier to entry that provides visible evidence of tampering if breached or missing, and this feature must be distinctive by design—meaning it cannot be duplicated with commonly available materials or processes—and must remain intact during handling in manufacture, distribution, and retail display [2].

The labeling requirement mandates a prominent statement on each retail package (except aerosol products) that alerts consumers to the specific tamper-resistant feature of the package. This statement must be placed so that it remains visible even if the tamper-resistant feature is breached or missing. If the tamper-resistant feature uses an identifying characteristic (e.g., a pattern, name, logo), that characteristic must be referenced in the labeling statement [3].

The requirement applies to all cosmetic liquid oral hygiene products packaged for retail sale on or after February 7, 1983, except for vaginal tablets, and is effective as of May 5, 1983 for vaginal tablets, with full compliance required by February 6, 1984 for products held for sale on or after that date [10][12][13]. However, the requirement does not apply to aerosol products, which are defined as those depending on liquefied or compressed gas to expel contents [2].

The exception in §700.25(e)(1)(i) and (ii) allows for a delay in implementation for certain product types, but this does not exempt mouthwash from the requirement if it is sold on open shelves [10][12]. The only way to avoid the tamper-resistant packaging requirement would be through a formally requested exemption under §700.25(d), which must include the name of the product, reasons why compliance is unnecessary or unachievable, and other information justifying an exemption [5][6][7].

These provisions impose no restriction on the type of mouthwash (e.g., flavor, concentration) beyond what is required by the labeling and tamper evidence standards. The requirement does not apply to products that are not accessible to the public while held for sale, such as those sold behind a counter or in sealed, non-accessible containers [2].

The available regulatory sources do not provide enough information to answer whether mouthwash sold on open shelves is subject to additional restrictions beyond tamper-resistant packaging and labeling.

asked: An auditor asks when the tamper-resistant packaging and labeling requirements took effect for our mouthwash and our vaginal tablets. What does the rule state?
answer:
The tamper-resistant packaging and labeling requirements for mouthwash and vaginal tablets took effect on different dates depending on the product type and specific requirement:

- For mouthwash: The packaging requirement (tamper-resistant package) became effective on February 7, 1983, for products packaged for retail sale on or after that date, except for the requirement that the indicator or barrier to entry be distinctive by design, which is not specified in this provision [10].  
- For vaginal tablets: The packaging requirement became effective on May 5, 1983, for products packaged for retail sale on or after that date [11].  
- The labeling requirement (including the statement about the tamper-resistant feature) was effective on February 6, 1984, for all affected cosmetic products packaged for retail sale on or after that date, except that the specific reference to an identifying characteristic in the label is required only from that date onward [12].  
- For products held for sale after February 6, 1984, the tamper-resistant packaging requirement applies as of that date, even if packaged before May 5, 1983, but this does not apply to the distinctive design requirement [13].

The rule states that the effective dates are tied to when a product is packaged for retail sale and depend on whether it is a mouthwash or vaginal tablet. The packaging requirement applies as of February 7, 1983 (for mouthwash) and May 5, 1983 (for vaginal tablets), while labeling requirements apply with specific dates tied to the type of product and the presence of an identifying characteristic [10][11][12][13].

21 CFR 700.25(e)(1)(i): The packaging requirement for mouthwash is effective on February 7, 1983, for products packaged for retail sale on or after that date, except for the distinctive indicator or barrier to entry requirement [10].

asked: We import a finished cream from Europe that contains cattle-derived ingredients. What must we do at entry, and what records must we produce?
answer:
At entry into the United States, an importer of a finished cream from Europe containing cattle-derived ingredients must affirm that the cream was manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise contains cattle material and that it was manufactured in accordance with 21 CFR 700.27. If requested by U.S. Customs and Border Protection, the importer must provide records within five days sufficient to demonstrate that the cosmetic is not manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise contains prohibited cattle materials. These records must be retained for two years after they were created. The cream may contain tallow provided it contains no more than 0.15 percent insoluble impurities as determined by AOCS Official Method Ca 3a-46 or an equivalent method. No cosmetic shall be manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise contain prohibited cattle materials, which include specified risk materials, small intestine of all cattle (except under specific conditions), material from nonambulatory disabled cattle, material from cattle not inspected and passed, or mechanically separated beef. The records required must establish that the cream is not manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise contains any prohibited cattle materials.

21 CFR 700.27(a)(1) defines prohibited cattle materials as specified risk materials, small intestine of all cattle (except under paragraph (b)(2)), material from nonambulatory disabled cattle, material from cattle not inspected and passed, or mechanically separated beef [2].  
21 CFR 700.27(a)(4) defines nonambulatory disabled cattle as those that cannot rise from a recumbent position or walk [7].  
21 CFR 700.27(a)(5) defines specified risk materials as brain, skull, eyes, trigeminal ganglia, spinal cord, vertebral column (excluding tail vertebrae and transverse processes), dorsal root ganglia of cattle 30 months or older, and tonsils and distal ileum of the small intestine of all cattle [8].  
21 CFR 700.27(a)(6) requires tallow to be produced from tissues that are not prohibited cattle materials or must contain no more than 0.15 percent insoluble impurities as determined by AOCS Official Method Ca 3a-46 or an equivalent method [9].  
21 CFR 700.27(a)(1)(i) excludes tallow with no more than 0.15% insoluble impurities, gelatin, hides and hide-derived products, milk and milk products, and materials inspected and passed from a designated country [3].  
21 CFR 700.27(b)(1) prohibits any cosmetic from being manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise containing prohibited cattle materials [13].  
21 CFR 700.27(c)(1) requires manufacturers and processors of a cosmetic containing cattle material to establish and maintain records sufficient to demonstrate that the product does not contain prohibited cattle materials [15].  
21 CFR 700.27(c)(2) mandates that such records be retained for two years after creation [16].  
21 CFR 700.27(c)(6) requires the importer of record to affirm, upon filing entry with U.S. Customs and Border Protection, that the cosmetic was manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise contains cattle material and was manufactured in accordance with this section; if requested, must provide records within five days demonstrating compliance [17].

asked: Our 'Avocado & Shea Hand Cream' has 12 ingredients, including avocado oil and shea butter, all listed on the back. Could the name still be misleading?
answer:
The name "Avocado & Shea Hand Cream" could be misleading under 21 CFR 701.1(b) because the label names the product after two ingredients—avocado and shea—but does not list all ingredients, even though the cream contains more than just these two. The provision specifically addresses labeling that suggests inclusion of one or more ingredients when not all are present, which may constitute a misleading representation [2].

21 CFR 701.1(b) prohibits labeling a cosmetic with a name that implies the presence of certain ingredients (like avocado and shea) if those ingredients are not all included in the product, even though the full list of ingredients is stated elsewhere on the label [2]. This means the name "Avocado & Shea Hand Cream" may be misleading because it suggests the product contains only these two ingredients or implies a focus on them when other ingredients are also present. The misbranding occurs if the name suggests inclusion of one or more but not all ingredients, which is prohibited under this regulation [2].

asked: Our required label information is printed in tiny light-gray type on silver foil on the jar bottom. Could FDA find it not prominent enough?
answer:
Yes, FDA could find the required label information not prominent enough because the smallness or style of type in which such information appears—specifically, tiny light-gray type on silver foil at the jar bottom—would constitute an insufficiency of prominence due to insufficient background contrast and crowding with other written or graphic matter. This is addressed under 21 CFR 701.2(a)(6), which identifies smallness or style of type, insufficient background contrast, and obscuring designs as factors that may render required information not prominent enough [7].

21 CFR 701.2(a)(6) specifies that smallness or style of type in which such word, statement, or information appears, insufficient background contrast, obscuring designs or vignettes, or crowding with other written, printed, or graphic matter may result in a failure to meet the prominence and conspicuousness required by section 602(c) of the Act [7].

asked: Our eyeshadow line has 20 shades on the same base, sold under one brand. Can one ingredient list with 'may contain' for colors cover all of them?
answer:
Yes, one ingredient list with "may contain" for colors can cover all 20 shades of eyeshadow sold under one brand, provided that: (1) the product line shares a common trade name or brand designation, and (2) no individual shade has a different brand or trade name appearing in its labeling. This is permitted under 21 CFR 701.3(g)(2)(iii), which allows a single ingredient declaration to apply to all products sold under a common brand if they share the same ingredient list and no distinct brand designation appears on any individual product [3]. Additionally, the list may include "may contain" statements for ingredients not present in the product, as allowed by 21 CFR 701.3(g) [2], provided that such declarations are made only when the ingredient is identified by the phrase “may contain” and all products share a common brand or trade name [3].

21 CFR 701.3(b) requires that the declaration of ingredients appear with prominence and conspicuousness, in letters not less than 1/16 of an inch in height, and may be placed on a tag, tape, or card if space is insufficient on the package [1].  
21 CFR 701.3(g) permits a declaration to include an ingredient not present in the product if it is identified by the phrase “may contain” [2].  
21 CFR 701.3(g)(2)(iii) requires that all products sharing the common declaration must be sold under a common trade name or brand designation, and no individual product may have a different trade name or brand designation in its labeling [3].  
21 CFR 701.3(o)(1) allows for a single list of ingredients common to all products in an assortment (e.g., eyeshadows of different colors), with a statement identifying the other ingredients and specifying which products contain them, provided the list is not misleading and is as informative as practicable [11].  
21 CFR 701.3(o)(2) permits a single ingredient list for products sold together in the same package if the total surface area available for labeling is less than 12 square inches [12].  

The available regulatory sources do not provide enough information to determine whether "may contain" statements can be used for colorants specifically, as no provision addresses colorant presence or absence. However, since the question involves a single brand with multiple shades and common formulation, the conditions in 701.3(g)(2)(iii) and (o)(1) support the use of one ingredient list with "may contain" if all products share the same brand name and no individual shade has a different trade name [3][11].  

Note: The requirement that the declaration must be conspicuous, in letters not less than 1/16 inch, applies generally to all ingredient declarations [1], but does not restrict the use of "may contain" for colorants.

Yes, one ingredient list with "may contain" for colors can cover all 20 shades of eyeshadow sold under one brand, provided that: (1) the product line shares a common trade name or brand designation, and (2) no individual shade has a different brand or trade name appearing in its labeling. This is permitted under 21 CFR 701.3(g)(2)(iii), which allows a single ingredient declaration to apply to all products sold under a common brand if they share the same ingredient list and no distinct brand designation appears on any individual product [3]. Additionally, the list may include "may contain" statements for ingredients not present in the product, as allowed by 21 CFR 701.3(g) [2], provided that such declarations are made only when the ingredient is identified by the phrase “may contain” and all products share a common brand or trade name [3].

21 CFR 701.3(b) requires that the declaration of ingredients appear with prominence and conspicuousness, in letters not less than 1/16 of an inch in height, and may be placed on a tag, tape, or card if space is insufficient on the package [1].  
21 CFR 701.3(g) permits a declaration to include an ingredient not present in the product if it is identified by the phrase “may contain” [2].  
21 CFR 701.3(g)(2)(iii) requires that all products sharing the common declaration must be sold under a common trade name or brand designation, and no individual product may have a different trade name or brand designation in its labeling [3].  
21 CFR 701.3(o)(1) allows for a single list of ingredients common to all products in an assortment (e.g., eyeshadows of different colors), with a statement identifying the other ingredients and specifying which products contain them, provided the list is not misleading and is as informative as practicable [11].  
21 CFR 701.3(o)(2) permits a single ingredient list for products sold together in the same package if the total surface area available for labeling is less than 12 square inches [12].  

The available regulatory sources do not provide enough information to determine whether "may contain" statements can be used for colorants specifically, as no provision addresses colorant presence or absence. However, since the question involves a single brand with multiple shades and common formulation, the conditions in 701.3(g)(2)(iii) and (o)(1) support the use of one ingredient list with "may contain" if all products share the same brand name and no individual shade has a different trade name [3][11].  

Note: The requirement that the declaration must be conspicuous, in letters not less than 1/16 inch, applies generally to all ingredient declarations [1], but does not restrict the use of "may contain" for colorants.

asked: Part of a bulk lotion shipment held at our own labeling plant left the plant mislabeled. What happens to the labeling exemption?
answer:
The labeling exemption for the bulk lotion shipment held at the plant is void ab initio if the cosmetic is mislabeled, as misbranding constitutes a violation that terminates the exemption under the conditions specified in 21 CFR 701.9(d)(1) and 701.9(b). The exemption does not survive once the cosmetic is found to be misbranded during removal from the establishment.

The labeling exemption for a shipment of bulk lotion held at a labeling plant is conditional upon the presence of a written agreement between the person who introduced the shipment and the operator of the establishment where it is processed, labeled, or repacked. This agreement must specify processing, labeling, or repacking details that ensure the cosmetic will not be adulterated or misbranded upon completion of such actions. If the shipment is mislabeled, the exemption becomes void ab initio as a result of the misbranding, per 21 CFR 701.9(d)(1). 

The exemption does not apply if the person who introduced the shipment into interstate commerce refuses to make available for inspection a copy of the written agreement required under paragraph (a)(2), which would cause the exemption to become void ab initio with respect to that person, as specified in 21 CFR 701.9(c). 

The requirement that such an agreement be kept by both parties until two years after the final shipment or delivery from the establishment is mandated under 21 CFR 701.9(a)(2), and copies must be made available for inspection at any reasonable hour upon request, as required in 21 CFR 701.9(a)(2). 

The exemption does not apply if the cosmetic is mislabeled during movement or holding because such misbranding triggers immediate voidance of the exemption under 21 CFR 701.9(d)(1), regardless of whether the agreement was properly executed or maintained.

asked: Our product is named 'Midnight Muse.' Is that enough as the statement of identity on the front panel?
answer:
The name "Midnight Muse" is not sufficient as a statement of identity on the front panel of a cosmetic product because 21 CFR 701.11(b) requires the statement of identity to be either the common or usual name of the cosmetic, an appropriately descriptive name, a fanciful name understood by the public when the nature of the cosmetic is obvious, or an appropriate illustration or vignette. The provision does not establish that "Midnight Muse" meets any of these criteria, and no source confirms that such a name qualifies as a fanciful name understood by the public [4]. The requirement for the statement of identity to be presented in bold type and in a size reasonably related to the most prominent printed matter on the panel applies, but does not establish acceptance of "Midnight Muse" as an identity [1].

The common or usual name of the cosmetic shall be used as the statement of identity [3].  
An appropriately descriptive name or, when the nature of the cosmetic is obvious, a fanciful name understood by the public to identify such cosmetic may be used [4].  
An appropriate illustration or vignette representing the intended cosmetic use may serve as the statement of identity [5].  

The available regulatory sources do not provide enough information to determine whether "Midnight Muse" qualifies as a fanciful name understood by the public in this context.

asked: How does § 710.3 say to register a cosmetic establishment?
answer:
To register a cosmetic establishment, an entity must obtain Form FD-2511 (“Registration of Cosmetic Product Establishment”) from the Food and Drug Administration at 5001 Campus Dr., College Park, MD 20740, or from any FDA district office, and then mail the completed form to Cosmetic Product Establishment Registration, Food and Drug Administration, 5001 Campus Dr., College Park, MD 20740 [1].

Form FD-2511 is the required form for registering a cosmetic establishment [1].

While a permanent registration number is assigned to a cosmetic product establishment upon registration [1], the text provides no authorization for the use of the phrase "FDA Registered Facility, Reg. No. ____" on packaging. The provision only states that the Commissioner will provide a validated copy of Form FD-2511 as evidence of registration, and this document is sent to the location shown for the registering establishment [1]. There is no requirement or authorization in 21 CFR 710.6 for such labeling on product cartons.

The available regulatory sources do not provide enough information to answer whether such a statement complies with FDA labeling requirements beyond what is specified in 21 CFR 710.6.

- The provision defines "prohibited cattle materials" (e.g., brain, small intestine of all cattle, nonambulatory disabled cattle, mechanically separated beef) and prohibits their use in cosmetics [2].  
- It requires that no cosmetic shall be manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise contain prohibited cattle materials [13].  
- Manufacturers must establish and maintain records to demonstrate the cosmetic does not contain prohibited cattle materials if it is made from, processed with, or contains material from cattle [16].  
- Tallow used in cosmetics must come from tissues that are not prohibited cattle materials or must contain no more than 0.15 percent insoluble impurities as determined by AOCS method Ca 3a-46 [9].  
- The small intestine is not considered prohibited if at least 80 inches of the distal ileum are removed proximally from the caeco-colic junction [14].  
- Adulteration occurs when a manufacturer or processor fails to comply with paragraphs (b) or (c), rendering the cosmetic adulterated under section 601(c) of the FD&C Act [17].

None of these provisions address contamination by rodent droppings, nor do they regulate recycled resin from non-cattle sources. Therefore, the presence of rodent droppings and unknown makeup of recycled resin are not governed by any specific requirement or prohibition in 21 CFR 700.27 as written. The regulation does not establish requirements for handling biological contaminants (e.g., rodents), nor does it define adulteration due to non-cattle organic contamination, such as from recycled resins or rodent excreta.

Thus, the provisions of 21 CFR 700.27 do not apply to rodent droppings in a lotion warehouse or to the use of a recycled resin of unknown makeup derived from non-animal sources. The question involves contamination unrelated to prohibited cattle materials and is outside the scope of these specific regulations.

asked: Our serum is sold in a retail box. What does the misbranding section require the label to carry?
answer:
The misbranding section requires that, for a cosmetic sold in a retail box (i.e., package form), the label must contain: (1) the name and place of business of the manufacturer, packer, or distributor; (2) an accurate statement of the quantity of the contents in terms of weight, measure, or numerical count; and (3) the information required under section 364e of this title. This requirement applies unless exemptions are established by regulations prescribed by the Secretary for small packages, which may permit reasonable variations in the labeling. These requirements are part of what constitutes misbranding under FD&C Act § 602(b), and failure to meet them would constitute a misbranded cosmetic.

FD&C Act § 602(b) [21 U.S.C. 362(b)] requires that, for package form cosmetics, the label must contain (1) the name and place of business of the manufacturer, packer, or distributor; (2) an accurate statement of the quantity of the contents in terms of weight, measure, or numerical count; and (3) the information required under section 364e of this title. Reasonable variations are permitted under clause (2), and exemptions for small packages may be established by regulations prescribed by the Secretary [3].

asked: A customer reports a second-degree burn after using our at-home peel as directed. Is it a 'serious adverse event', and who is the 'responsible person'?
answer:
A second-degree burn after use of an at-home peel as directed constitutes a serious adverse event because it meets the definition of "significant disfigurement" under conditions of use that are customary or usual, as specified in FD&C Act § 604(5)(vii)[6]. The responsible person is the manufacturer, packer, or distributor of the cosmetic product whose name appears on the label of such cosmetic product in accordance with section 364e(a) of this title or section 1453(a) of title 15, as defined in FD&C Act § 604(4)[5].

FD&C Act § 604(5)(vii)[6] defines a serious adverse event to include "significant disfigurement (including serious and persistent rashes, second- or third-degree burns, significant hair loss, or persistent or significant alteration of appearance), other than as intended, under conditions of use that are customary or usual."

FD&C Act § 604(4)[5] defines the term "responsible person" to mean the manufacturer, packer, or distributor of a cosmetic product whose name appears on the label of such cosmetic product in accordance with section 364e(a) of this title or section 1453(a) of title 15.

asked: How long must we keep adverse event records for our skin creams, and who may see them during an inspection?
answer:
Adverse event records for skin creams must be kept for 6 years by most responsible persons, except for small businesses that do not engage in manufacturing or processing of cosmetic products described in section 364h(b) of the FD&C Act, which are exempt and only required to maintain such records for 3 years. During an inspection, access to these records is permitted for officers or employees of the Department of Health and Human Services who have appropriate credentials as determined by the Secretary and have been duly designated by the Secretary to have access to the records [3].

Records related to adverse events must be maintained for a period of 6 years, except that a small business not engaged in manufacturing or processing of cosmetic products described in subsection 364h(b) shall maintain such records for only 3 years [3].  
Access to these records during an inspection is permitted for an authorized person, defined as an officer or employee of the Department of Health and Human Services who has appropriate credentials as determined by the Secretary and has been duly designated by the Secretary to have access to the records [3].
