asked: We're the brand owner of a new face serum made by a contract lab. What does the FD&C Act require us to have on safety before and while we market it?
answer:
The FD&C Act requires that a brand owner of a face serum made by a contract lab ensure and maintain records supporting adequate substantiation of safety of the product before and while marketing it. This includes maintaining evidence that the product is safe under the conditions of use prescribed in the labeling or customary/usual conditions, where "safe" means not injurious to users, and minor transient reactions do not constitute injury. The requirement for adequate substantiation of safety involves tests, studies, research, analyses, or other evidence considered sufficient by experts qualified by scientific training and experience to evaluate the safety of cosmetic products and their ingredients. The requirement may consider cumulative or relevant exposure to the product or ingredient when determining safety. 

FD&C Act § 608(a) [21 U.S.C. 364d(a)] requires a responsible person for a cosmetic product to ensure and maintain records supporting adequate substantiation of safety of such product.  
FD&C Act § 608(c)(1) [21 U.S.C. 364d(c)(1)] defines "adequate substantiation of safety" as tests or studies, research, analyses, or other evidence considered sufficient by experts qualified by scientific training and experience to evaluate the safety of cosmetic products and their ingredients.  
FD&C Act § 608(c)(2) [21 U.S.C. 364d(c)(2)] defines "safe" as meaning the product is not injurious under the conditions of use prescribed in labeling or customary/usual conditions, and the Secretary shall not consider a cosmetic ingredient or product injurious solely because it causes minor and transient reactions or irritations in some users.  
FD&C Act § 608(c)(3) [21 U.S.C. 364d(c)] allows consideration of cumulative or other relevant exposure to the cosmetic product, including any ingredient, when determining whether a product is safe.  

The requirement does not apply to coal-tar hair dye if it otherwise complies with section 361(a), as specified in FD&C Act § 608(b) [21 U.S.C. 364d(b)].  
The responsible person for the face serum, defined as the manufacturer, packer, or distributor whose name appears on the label, is required to maintain records supporting safety substantiation, per FD&C Act § 604(4) [21 U.S.C. 364(4)].

asked: FDA arrived with written notice, asking for records on a shampoo it believes is contaminated and dangerous. What must we provide?
answer:
If the FDA delivers a written notice requesting records on a shampoo it believes is contaminated and dangerous, the responsible person and facility must permit an FDA officer or employee, upon presentation of appropriate credentials and a written notice, to have access to and copy all records relating to that cosmetic product and any other cosmetic product the Secretary reasonably believes is likely to be affected in a similar manner, provided such records are needed to assist the Secretary in determining whether the cosmetic product is adulterated and presents a threat of serious adverse health consequences or death to humans. Access must occur at reasonable times and within reasonable limits and in a reasonable manner. The request must be made by an officer or employee duly designated by the Secretary.

The provision requires access to and copying of all records relating to the cosmetic product and any other cosmetic product the Secretary reasonably believes is likely to be affected in a similar manner [1].  
Access is permitted only if the records are needed to assist the Secretary in determining whether the cosmetic product is adulterated and presents a threat of serious adverse health consequences or death to humans [1].  
The request must be made by an officer or employee duly designated by the Secretary, upon presentation of appropriate credentials and a written notice [1].  
Access occurs at reasonable times and within reasonable limits and in a reasonable manner [1].  
Records that are excluded include recipes or formulas for cosmetics, financial data, pricing data, personnel data (other than data as to qualification of technical and professional personnel performing functions subject to this chapter), research data (other than safety substantiation data for cosmetic products and their ingredients), and sales data (other than shipment data regarding sales) [1].  
The requirement does not extend to records related to a facility that solely performs labeling, relabeling, packaging, repackaging, holding, or distributing of cosmetic products if such activities are not part of the manufacturing or processing of a product for retail sale [1].

asked: We're a contract filler; the brand owner is the responsible person. Do the 610 record-access duties apply to us?
answer:
Yes, the 610 record-access duties apply to contract fillers when the brand owner is the responsible person, because § 610(a) applies to each responsible person and facility, and if the brand owner is listed on the label as the responsible person under § 604(4), then that person and any facility involved in manufacturing or processing cosmetics are subject to record access requirements [1].  

The record-access duties under FD&C Act § 610(a) apply to each responsible person and facility when the Secretary has a reasonable belief that a cosmetic product is likely to be adulterated in a manner posing a threat of serious adverse health consequences or death [1].  

The record-access duties do not extend to recipes or formulas, financial data, pricing data, personnel data (other than data on qualification of technical and professional personnel), research data (except safety substantiation data for cosmetics and ingredients), or sales data (except shipment data regarding sales) [1].  

The record-access duty applies only if the Secretary has a reasonable belief that a cosmetic product is likely to be adulterated and poses a threat of serious adverse health consequences or death; otherwise, no access is required under § 610(a) [1].  

The record-access duty applies to any facility that manufactures or processes cosmetic products, including contract fillers engaged in such activities, as long as they are not excluded by § 604(3)(B), which excludes entities performing only labeling, relabeling, packaging, repackaging, holding, or distributing without manufacturing or processing [1].

These provisions do not require any specific retention period for records beyond what is necessary to assist the Secretary in determining adulteration [1].

asked: FDA says our talc body powder may be adulterated and could cause serious harm. Can FDA force us to stop distribution or recall?
answer:
Yes, FDA can force a company to stop distribution or recall talc body powder if the Secretary determines there is a reasonable probability that the product is adulterated or misbranded and use of or exposure to it could cause serious adverse health consequences or death. This authority is granted under FD&C Act § 611(a), which allows the Secretary to issue an order requiring immediate cessation of distribution or recall, even if the responsible person refuses to act voluntarily [1].

The authority to require cessation of distribution or recall is established in FD&C Act § 611(a) [21 U.S.C. 364g(a)], which provides that if the Secretary determines there is a reasonable probability that a cosmetic is adulterated or misbranded and exposure could cause serious adverse health consequences or death, the Secretary may issue an order requiring immediate cessation of distribution or recall, even if the responsible person refuses to act voluntarily [1].

The responsible person must be given an opportunity for an informal hearing within 10 days after the issuance of the order to determine whether adequate evidence justifies the order, as specified in FD&C Act § 611(b) [21 U.S.C. 364g(b)] [2].

If the Secretary issues a recall or distribution cessation order, the responsible person must immediately cease distribution or recall the product and provide notification as required by the order, as mandated in FD&C Act § 611(d) [21 U.S.C. 364g(d)] [4].

The Secretary may also require the responsible person to notify appropriate persons—including manufacturers, distributors, importers, and retailers—and the public about the recall or cessation of distribution, as specified in FD&C Act § 611(e) [21 U.S.C. 364g(e)] [5].

In conducting a recall, the Secretary shall ensure that a press release is published and alerts are issued to consumers and retailers, including details such as the name of the product, description of the risk, and information about similar non-affected products, as required in FD&C Act § 611(f) [21 U.S.C. 364g(f)] [6].

The authority to issue a recall order is not delegated; it must be exercised by the Commissioner, as stated in FD&C Act § 611(g) [21 U.S.C. 364g(g)] [7].

Nothing in this section limits or affects the Secretary’s ability to request or participate in a voluntary recall, or to issue an order under any other provision of the subchapter, per FD&C Act § 611(h) [21 U.S.C. 364g(h)] [8].

raw:
Yes, FDA can force a company to stop distribution or recall talc body powder if the Secretary determines there is a reasonable probability that the product is adulterated or misbranded and use of or exposure to it could cause serious adverse health consequences or death. This authority is granted under FD&C Act § 611(a), which allows the Secretary to issue an order requiring a responsible person to immediately cease distribution or recall the product if they refuse or do not voluntarily comply within the time and manner prescribed by the Secretary [1].

The authority to require cessation of distribution or recall is established in FD&C Act § 611(a) [21 U.S.C. 364g(a)], which provides that if the Secretary determines there is a reasonable probability that a cosmetic is adulterated or misbranded and exposure could cause serious adverse health consequences or death, the Secretary may issue an order requiring immediate cessation of distribution or recall, even if the responsible person refuses to act voluntarily [1].

The responsible person must be given an opportunity for an informal hearing within 10 days after the issuance of the order to determine whether adequate evidence justifies the order, as specified in FD&C Act § 611(b) [21 U.S.C. 364g(b)] [2].

If the Secretary issues a recall or distribution cessation order, the responsible person must immediately cease distribution or recall the product and provide notification as required by the order, as mandated in FD&C Act § 611(d) [21 U.S.C. 364g(d)] [4].

The Secretary may also require the responsible person to notify appropriate persons—including manufacturers, distributors, importers, and retailers—and the public about the recall or cessation of distribution, as specified in FD&C Act § 611(e) [21 U.S.C. 364g(e)] [5].

In conducting a recall, the Secretary shall ensure that a press release is published and alerts are issued to consumers and retailers, including details such as the name of the product, description of the risk, and information about similar non-affected products, as required in FD&C Act § 611(f) [21 U.S.C. 364g(f)] [6].

The authority to issue a recall order is not delegated; it must be exercised by the Commissioner, as stated in FD&C Act § 611(g) [21 U.S.C. 364g(g)] [7].

Nothing in this section limits or affects the Secretary’s ability to request or participate in a voluntary recall, or to issue an order under any other provision of the subchapter, per FD&C Act § 611(h) [21 U.S.C. 364g(h)] [8].

These provisions impose no requirement for specific labeling, ingredient disclosure, or product testing beyond what is required by sections 361 and 362 of the FD&C Act; however, they do establish a legal pathway for FDA to mandate recall or cessation based on risk of serious harm. The authority depends on the Secretary’s determination that there is a reasonable probability of adulteration or misbranding and that exposure could cause serious adverse health consequences or death [1].

asked: A state wants cosmetic facilities to register with it under its own rules. Can it impose registration requirements different from federal ones?
answer:
A state cannot impose registration requirements for cosmetic facilities that differ from or are in addition to federal requirements applicable under the FD&C Act, as such actions would violate the preemption provisions established in section 614(a). Specifically, no State or political subdivision may establish or continue any law, regulation, order, or other requirement for cosmetics that is different from or in addition to, or otherwise not identical with, any federal requirement regarding registration and product listing. This includes requirements related to registration of cosmetic facilities [1].

The FD&C Act § 614(a) [21 U.S.C. 364j(a)] prohibits states from imposing registration requirements different from federal ones [1].  

The available regulatory sources do not provide enough information to answer whether a state may impose other types of non-registration requirements (e.g., inspection, licensing, or fees), as the question specifically concerns registration and only the provision on registration is directly relevant. The text does not address non-registration requirements beyond what is stated in § 614(a).

asked: Our product contains beef tallow. What records must we keep to show the cattle material is acceptable, and must we hold lots in quarantine until verified?
answer:
To show that beef tallow is acceptable for use in a cosmetic product, manufacturers must establish and maintain records sufficient to demonstrate that the tallow contains no more than 0.15 percent insoluble impurities as determined by AOCS Official Method Ca 3a-46 or an equivalent method, and that it is not derived from prohibited cattle materials. These records must be retained for 2 years after creation. When filing entry with U.S. Customs and Border Protection, the importer of record must affirm that the cosmetic was manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise contains cattle material and was manufactured in accordance with this section, and if requested, must provide records within five days to demonstrate the absence of prohibited cattle materials. The evidence does not contain any requirement to hold lots in quarantine until verified.

21 CFR 700.27(a)(6) requires tallow to be produced from tissues that are not prohibited cattle materials or must contain no more than 0.15 percent insoluble impurities as determined by AOCS Official Method Ca 3a-46 or an equivalent method [8].  
21 CFR 700.27(c)(1) requires manufacturers and processors of a cosmetic that is manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise contains material from cattle to establish and maintain records sufficient to demonstrate that the cosmetic is not manufactured from, processed with, or does not otherwise contain prohibited cattle materials [14].  
21 CFR 700.27(c)(2) requires that such records must be retained for 2 years after the date they were created [15].  
21 CFR 700.27(c)(6) requires, when filing entry with U.S. Customs and Border Protection, that the importer of record affirm that the cosmetic was manufactured from, processed with, or otherwise contains cattle material and was manufactured in accordance with this section, and if requested, must provide records within five days to demonstrate the absence of prohibited cattle materials [17].

However, no provision in 21 CFR 80.39 authorizes or specifies the demand for employees' training and qualification files. The requirement applies only to records showing disposal of color additives, including quantities used and shipments made, and these records must be kept separately from other records [3][4]. 

The requested provision does not authorize FDA to demand employees’ training and qualification files under 21 CFR 80.39. These provisions impose no requirement for such files to be provided by a contract manufacturer to an FDA investigator. The available sources do not provide any authority or condition under which FDA may require training and qualification records of employees beyond the specific color additive distribution records outlined in (b)(1) and (b)(2), nor do they establish conditions permitting access to personnel training or qualification files [3][4]. 

Therefore, based on 21 CFR 80.39:  
- FDA may not demand employees' training and qualification files under this provision; the regulation does not authorize such a request.  
- The only records required are those related to color additive distribution, including quantities used and shipments made [3][4].  
- These records must be available upon request by an FDA officer or employee acting on behalf of the Secretary of Health and Human Services, at all reasonable hours until at least 2 years after disposal of such additives [1].  
- The records required are limited to distribution data and must be kept separately from other records [5].  

Note: The provision does not address personnel training or qualification files for employees. Any request for such files would fall outside the scope of 21 CFR 80.39, as no such requirement exists in the cited text.

The 3PL is not required to register with the FDA under 21 CFR 700.3(b) [5]; this provision defines "cosmetic product" as a finished cosmetic whose manufacture has been completed and does not establish any registration requirement for third-party holders.

A 3PL holding finished cosmetics without manufacturing, compounding, or selling them is exempt from registration under 21 CFR 710.9(a) [2], which exempts beauty shops, cosmetologists, retailers, pharmacies, and other persons who administer, dispense, or distribute cosmetic products at retail from a single location.

A 3PL holding finished cosmetics without manufacturing, compounding, or selling them is exempt from registration under 21 CFR 710.9(b) [3], which exempts physicians, hospitals, clinics, and public health agencies.

A 3PL holding finished cosmetics without manufacturing, compounding, or selling them is exempt from registration under 21 CFR 710.9(c) [4], which exempts persons who manufacture, prepare, compound, or process cosmetic products solely for use in research, pilot plant production, teaching, or chemical analysis and do not sell these products.

- The provision does not mandate any specific actions related to handling complaints, nor does it establish procedures for investigating them.

Therefore, based on the available evidence:

- Records of consumer complaints and adverse events are considered confidential data in color additive petitions and may be redacted to remove identifying information [4](i), [4](ii).  
- The regulation does not specify a retention period for such records.  
- There is no requirement under 21 CFR 71.15 for an indie brand to maintain a written complaint-handling SOP or to investigate every complaint.  

Note: The cited provisions relate specifically to color additive petitions and the confidentiality of data submitted in those petitions, not to general product safety complaints or adverse event reporting requirements applicable to food, drugs, or cosmetics under other FDA regulations. Thus, 21 CFR 71.15 does not address the specific questions about complaint handling, SOPs, or investigation obligations for an indie brand.
